sections.html:
Findlay is the Hancock County seat, about 40 miles south of Toledo, and the second-largest city in Northwest Ohio. The Blanchard River crosses town east to west, and subdivisions fill most of the 19.64 square miles of land. Marathon Petroleum, Whirlpool and the regional hospital supply many of the buyers.

An owner can hire an agent, go it alone, or deal with an investor directly. The local details below change the math for each, starting with the river.

About 40 percent of households rent, so landlords and first-time buyers both shop here. The population estimate for 2025 is 40,370, close to the 2020 count of 40,313, which means rival listings rather than newcomers cap what a house fetches.

Flood exposure is the first property-specific question Findlay buyers and lenders raise. The river crested at 18.46 feet in 2007, causing around $100 million in damage and coming close to the 1913 record. The city's floodplain page covers what an owner should know:

  • The city participates in the National Flood Insurance Program, so any parcel can be insured through it or a private carrier.
  • Grading, new construction and alterations inside a Special Flood Hazard Area need a Flood Development Permit before work begins.
  • Structural damage in that area, from flood, fire, wind or anything else, goes to the Zoning Department for a damage assessment.
  • The Hancock County Auditor maps show whether a given parcel sits in the hazard area, and zoning staff will help read them.

After the first phase of river benching, the city sent FEMA a Letter of Map Revision proposing to remove or shrink flood zones over a significant amount of land, and the city's flood information page links a parcel list. Check whether your lot is named before choosing a list price, since a revised map can lower or raise a buyer's insurance premium.

Weather tests the structure too. Findlay gets about 37.7 inches of precipitation and 23.8 inches of snow a year, so buyers poke at roof edges, downspouts and damp basement corners.

Marathon Petroleum has its headquarters downtown, Whirlpool runs what is considered the world's largest dishwasher plant by output, and several retailers operate distribution centers here. Blanchard Valley Regional Health Center is the largest local employer, and the University of Findlay and Owens Community College add students and staff to the buyer pool.

Interstate 75 crosses the city, US 68 ends here, and US 224 plus Ohio routes 12, 15, 37 and 568 all pass through. Public school students attend Findlay City Schools, and Findlay High School covers grades 9 to 12. Plant, hospital and university employees tend to want a short drive, so lead with commute and school details in a listing.

sections.h2: Hancock County deed transfer and recording
sections.html:
The county Auditor takes $3 for every thousand dollars conveyed, rounded to the nearest ten cents, and adds $0.50 per parcel. Some transfers are exempt from the conveyance portion.

The Auditor needs a DTE 100 statement of value, or a DTE 100(EX) when an exemption applies, and a notarized deed whose legal description is exact. Write checks to the Hancock County Auditor. Staff in the Real Estate Division, room 21 of the courthouse, take questions at 419-424-7015.

Filing with the recorder comes next. The recorder charges $39 for the first two pages of a document and $8 for each additional page, a rate that began in January 2025. Ohio requires the signature on the deed to be acknowledged before a notary or similar officer (ORC 5301.01).

sections.h2: What a Findlay seller hands the buyer
sections.html:
Ohio's residential disclosure statute (ORC 5302.30) has the seller fill in a condition form for the buyer. Late delivery opens a three business day window for the buyer to walk away. The statute exempts estate fiduciaries, heirs who never lived in the home and family transfers, a list that fits Findlay's many long-held family houses.

If the house sits near the river, attach any elevation certificate, flood insurance record or sump-pump history to the form. Documents answer the flood question before a buyer asks it.

sections.h2: Practical ways to sell a Findlay house
sections.html:
Your repair list and your deadline decide which route fits.

  • Agent listing: the most exposure, with closing set by showings and the buyer's lender.
  • Sale by owner: no commission, but forms and deed prep are yours.
  • Cash purchase: no lender or appraisal, and you pick the closing day, at a price that reflects the repairs.
  • Family or neighbor sale: friendlier talks and the same Auditor paperwork.

Line up two written offers and compare what each leaves you after fees, tax proration and payoff.

sections.h2: Selling a long-held or rented Findlay house
sections.html:
Many Findlay houses have stayed in one family for decades, and that brings its own checklist. Find the deed first and confirm whose names are on it. If an owner has died, the person signing needs proof of authority, and the title company will tell you what it wants to see. An heir who never lived in the house may be exempt from the disclosure form, but a buyer will still ask about the roof, the basement and the furnace.

For a rental, read the lease for its end date and notice terms. Investors like a tenant who pays on time, and a buyer who wants to move in will need the house empty on a firm date. Say which kind of buyer you are after at the first showing, so you don't lose weeks to the wrong one.

sections.h2: From accepted offer to closing in Findlay
sections.html:
After the contract is signed, the title company checks the record and prepares the DTE form. Your part is to confirm the legal description on the deed is exact, since the Auditor won't accept a deed that gets it wrong, and to sign before a notary. Once the Auditor has endorsed the deed, it goes to the recorder. Until it is recorded, a deed is fraudulent against a later good-faith buyer (ORC 5301.25), so closers file fast.

Bring photo identification and any payoff letter for a mortgage. If the house is a rental, bring the lease. For an inherited house, bring the papers that show who may sign. A cash buyer skips the appraisal, so the closing day is yours to pick, but the deed and the county steps stay the same.

faqs.q: Does a Findlay home near the river sell for less?
faqs.a: It can, since flood insurance adds a cost for the buyer. Pull the parcel on the Hancock County Auditor maps, ask Zoning about the pending map revision, and keep any elevation certificate or insurance records handy.

faqs.q: What is the Hancock County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The Auditor charges $3 per $1,000 conveyed and $0.50 per parcel, with recording billed separately by the recorder. Call the Real Estate Division for the total on your deed.

faqs.q: Do I have to repair a Findlay house before selling?
faqs.a: Ohio sets no repair requirement for a sale. Known problems go on the disclosure form, and a lender-backed buyer may negotiate fixes after the inspection.

faqs.q: Where is the deed filed once a Findlay sale closes?
faqs.a: With the Hancock County Recorder, once the Auditor has endorsed it. Until recorded, a deed is fraudulent against a later good-faith buyer (ORC 5301.25), so closers file fast.

faqs.q: Who buys houses in Findlay besides families?
faqs.a: Landlords and investors do, since roughly 40 percent of households rent at a median of $975. Plant, hospital and university employees add to the buyer pool.
